title: Concurrent collections and channels
body: `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>`, `ConcurrentQueue<T>`, `ConcurrentStack<T>` and `ConcurrentBag<T>` are safe to use from many threads without external locks. Use their atomic compound operations: `GetOrAdd`, `AddOrUpdate`, `TryRemove`, `TryDequeue`. Note that the factory passed to `GetOrAdd` may run more than once under contention, even though only one value is stored.

`System.Threading.Channels` is the modern producer/consumer pipe. `Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity)` gives a writer and a reader; `await writer.WriteAsync(item)` waits when the channel is full, so a fast producer is slowed to the consumer's pace. That waiting is backpressure, and it keeps memory bounded. Unbounded channels never wait and can grow without limit.

Consumers use `await foreach (var item in reader.ReadAllAsync(token))`. The producer calls `writer.Complete()` when done, which ends the consumers' loops once the remaining items are drained. `Complete(exception)` propagates a failure to readers.

`BoundedChannelOptions` chooses what happens when full: `Wait` (backpressure, the default), `DropOldest`, `DropNewest` or `DropWrite`. `SingleReader`/`SingleWriter` hints enable faster implementations. Multiple consumers reading the same channel share the work; each item goes to exactly one reader.
Check that every channel is completed exactly once (or consumers wait forever), that cancellation stops both sides, and that bounded capacity matches how much memory you can afford.
expectedStdout:
a=3 b=2 c=1
producer waits at item 3
consumed total 10, reader completed: True
3 consumers shared the work: 5050
challenge: Build a two-stage pipeline: stage one writes the numbers 1..5 to a bounded channel of capacity 1; stage two reads them, squares them and writes to a second channel; the main code reads the second channel and prints the squares. Complete each channel when its writer finishes.
question: What does `await writer.WriteAsync(item)` do on a full bounded channel with FullMode.Wait?
correct: Waits until a reader makes room
reasoning: Waiting writers are backpressure: the producer runs no faster than the consumer, keeping memory bounded.
